description: Design and execute a tunnel boring project from ground investigation through TBM selection, face pressure management, segment design, and settlement monitoring.

steps.description: Plan and execute the ground investigation campaign needed before tunnel design: boreholes, CPT, geophysics, and groundwater characterization.

inputs.name: tunnel-alignment-corridor
inputs.desc: Proposed horizontal and vertical alignment corridor with surface constraints

inputs.name: tunnel-diameter-range
inputs.desc: Expected excavated diameter range from functional requirements

outputs.name: ground-model
outputs.desc: Interpreted geotechnical model along alignment: soil/rock stratigraphy, strength parameters, permeability, groundwater levels

outputs.name: investigation-risk-register
outputs.desc: Residual uncertainties in ground model with their spatial extent and consequence

process: Start with desk study: geological maps, historical boreholes, aerial photographs, and records of previous construction in the corridor.
Define borehole spacing by ground variability. 50 to 100 m spacing in uniform geology, 25 to 50 m at transitions, fault zones, or where cover is thin.

Select in-situ tests by ground type. CPTu for soft ground (provides continuous profile of qt, fs, u2). SPT in granular soils where CPT refusal occurs. Pressuremeter in rock for deformability. Vane shear in soft clay for undrained strength.

Plan laboratory program: classification tests on every sample, strength tests (UU, CU, CD triaxial) at intervals, consolidation tests in compressible layers, permeability tests in aquifers. Include abrasivity tests (CAI, LCPC) in rock for cutter life prediction.

Install piezometers at multiple depths to characterize groundwater regime: perched water, artesian pressures, tidal influence near coasts. Run pumping tests if dewatering or ground treatment is anticipated.
Run geophysical surveys (seismic refraction, MASW, ERT) between boreholes to interpolate stratigraphy and detect anomalies (voids, buried structures, boulders in glacial till).

Build interpreted ground model: longitudinal section along alignment with soil/rock units, strength envelopes, groundwater levels, and expected TBM behavior zones. Flag transitions between ground types as high-risk reaches.

steps.description: Select TBM type and specify its key parameters based on ground conditions, tunnel diameter, and alignment constraints.

inputs.name: ground-model
inputs.desc: Interpreted geotechnical model along alignment

inputs.name: tunnel-diameter-range
inputs.desc: Excavated diameter range from functional requirements

outputs.name: tbm-specification
outputs.desc: TBM type, diameter, thrust capacity, torque, cutterhead design, muck handling system, and backup system requirements

outputs.name: ground-conditioning-plan
outputs.desc: Conditioning agents and injection rates for each ground zone (foam, polymer, bentonite for EPB; slurry density targets for slurry shield)

process: Map ground zones to TBM types. EPB shield for soft ground (cohesive soils, mixed face with clay fraction above 10 to 15%). Slurry shield for granular soils below water table with high permeability (k > 1e-5 m/s) where EPB cannot maintain face support. Hard rock TBM (open or shielded) for rock with UCS above 25 MPa. For mixed face with rock and soil, dual-mode or hybrid TBM.

Size the cutterhead. Excavated diameter from internal diameter plus segment thickness plus tail void plus shield skin clearance. Typical segment thickness is tunnel radius divided by 10 to 12. Opening ratio of cutterhead face: 25 to 35% for clay, up to 50% for granular soil. Disc cutter spacing 70 to 90 mm for hard rock.

Calculate required thrust from face pressure plus friction. Face pressure equals groundwater pressure plus effective earth pressure (K0 * sigma_v_eff at axis, or higher if full overburden). Add skin friction along shield (empirical: 2 to 5 kN per m2 of shield surface). Total thrust must exceed this with margin for difficult ground.

Calculate required torque from cutterhead. Empirical methods: torque proportional to diameter cubed for soft ground, or sum of cutter forces times moment arms for rock. Installed torque typically 1.3 to 1.5 times calculated torque for breakout after stoppage.

Specify muck handling. For EPB: screw conveyor diameter (typically 0.6 to 0.7 m for 6 m diameter tunnel), screw length for pressure gradient (longer screw for higher face pressure), belt conveyor or muck car behind. For slurry: slurry circuit with separation plant (cyclones, screens, centrifuge for fine particles).

Define ground conditioning plan by zone. For EPB in clay: foam injection with FIR (foam injection ratio) 30 to 60%, FER (foam expansion ratio) 8 to 15. For EPB in sand: add polymer to increase fines adhesion, or bentonite slurry injection. For slurry shield: target slurry density 1.05 to 1.30 g/cm3 depending on permeability and face pressure.
Specify probe drilling and pre-excavation treatment capability. Forward probe drilling from cutterhead for ground investigation ahead. Pre-excavation grouting ports for mixed ground or fault zones.

steps.description: Design precast concrete tunnel lining segments: geometry, reinforcement, gaskets, and connection system.

inputs.name: tbm-specification
inputs.desc: TBM type, diameter, thrust capacity

inputs.name: ground-model
inputs.desc: Ground conditions along alignment including worst-case loading

outputs.name: segment-design
outputs.desc: Segment geometry (width, thickness, taper), reinforcement layout, gasket specification, bolt/dowel connections, and production tolerances

outputs.name: segment-structural-checks
outputs.desc: Structural verification for all load cases: ground loading, TBM thrust, handling, stacking, grouting pressure

process: Set ring geometry. Segment thickness from empirical rule: inner radius divided by 10 to 12, refined by structural analysis. Ring width typically 1.2 to 2.0 m (wider rings mean fewer joints but heavier segments; crane capacity and logistics constrain the choice). Typical ring: 5 segments plus key, or 6 plus key. Taper the ring for curve negotiation: taper equals ring width times sin(minimum curve angle per ring).

Determine design loads. Ground loading from analytical methods (Curtis-Muir Wood, Duddeck-Erdmann) or numerical analysis (2D FEM with beam-spring or continuum model). Include surcharge, adjacent structures, future development loads. Hydrostatic pressure at maximum groundwater level. TBM thrust jack forces on segment face (check local crushing at shoe pads). Grouting pressure behind segments (typically 1 to 3 bar above groundwater).

Design reinforcement. Primary reinforcement for bending moment and normal force from ground loading (interaction diagram). Splitting reinforcement at thrust jack locations (bursting forces from concentrated load). Edge reinforcement at gasket groove. Consider steel fiber reinforced concrete as alternative to rebar for standard segments (50 to 60 kg/m3 steel fibers, verify post-crack ductility).

Specify gasket system. EPDM gasket in groove near extrados face. Gasket design must maintain watertight seal at maximum gap and offset from construction tolerances. Gap from ring build accuracy and ground movement. Offset from ring roll and TBM steering. Gasket cross-section sized so compressed gasket contact stress exceeds water pressure at maximum gap and offset combination.

Design connection system. Bolts (straight or curved) or dowels between segments within a ring for handling and initial ring build. Dowel pins between rings to prevent ring roll during TBM advance. Guide rods to assist segment erection. Bolt pockets must not interfere with gasket groove or reinforcement. Specify hand-tightening torque for bolts to avoid over-compression of gasket.

Define production tolerances. Segment mold precision: length and width +/- 0.5 mm, thickness +/- 1 mm, gasket groove position +/- 0.5 mm. Concrete: f'c typically 50 to 60 MPa at 28 days, stripping strength at 8 to 12 hours. Curing regime for durability (steam cure or wet cure). Acceptance testing: dimensional check every segment, strength testing per batch.

Check handling and stacking loads. Segments must resist vacuum lifter handling forces and stacking loads during storage (typically 5 rings high). These transient load cases often govern reinforcement at segment edges.

steps.description: Set and control face pressure during TBM advance to prevent settlement and maintain face stability.

inputs.name: tbm-specification
inputs.desc: TBM type and ground conditioning plan

inputs.name: ground-model
inputs.desc: Ground conditions with groundwater pressures along alignment

outputs.name: face-pressure-regime
outputs.desc: Target face pressure profile along alignment with upper and lower limits and control parameters for each ground zone

outputs.name: intervention-protocol
outputs.desc: Procedures for hyperbaric interventions, cutterhead inspection, and tool changes under pressure

process: Calculate target face pressure for each chainage. Minimum: groundwater pressure plus active earth pressure at tunnel axis (prevents face collapse). Maximum: groundwater pressure plus at-rest earth pressure at crown plus safety margin (prevents blow-out). For shallow tunnels, check blow-out against overburden: face pressure must not exceed total vertical stress at crown minus a safety factor.

For EPB: face pressure is controlled by the balance between TBM advance rate (material intake) and screw conveyor extraction rate. Set target earth pressure at the bulkhead sensors. Muck conditioning must produce a paste with low permeability to maintain the pressure gradient across the screw. Monitor screw conveyor torque and discharge rate. If pressure drops: slow extraction, increase advance rate, inject bentonite. If pressure rises: increase extraction rate, reduce advance rate.

For slurry shield: face pressure is controlled by the slurry circuit. Pressurized slurry in the excavation chamber supports the face. Maintain slurry level and pressure via feed pump. Slurry density must form a filter cake on permeable ground to transfer pressure to the face. Monitor pressure difference between feed and return lines. Separation plant must maintain slurry density within specification by removing excavated material.

Define monitoring requirements. Continuous logging of face pressure, advance rate, screw torque (EPB) or slurry pressure and flow (slurry), grout pressure and volume, tail void grouting volume. Real-time display in TBM cabin with alarm limits. Typical alarm: face pressure deviating more than 0.2 to 0.5 bar from target.

Plan interventions. Compressed air interventions for cutterhead inspection and cutter changes. Calculate required intervention pressure from groundwater pressure at invert. Maximum intervention pressure limited by personnel safety (typically 3.5 bar, with saturation diving beyond that). Plan pre-treatment (ground freezing or grouting) for interventions in permeable ground where compressed air losses would be excessive.

steps.description: Predict ground settlement from tunneling and design the monitoring system to verify predictions and protect structures.

inputs.name: face-pressure-regime
inputs.desc: Target face pressure profile along alignment

inputs.name: ground-model
inputs.desc: Ground conditions and surface structures along alignment

outputs.name: settlement-predictions
outputs.desc: Predicted settlement trough at each critical section: maximum settlement, trough width, volume loss, angular distortion at structures

outputs.name: monitoring-plan
outputs.desc: Instrument layout, reading frequency, trigger levels (green/amber/red), and contingency actions

process: Predict the settlement trough using the Gaussian trough method (Peck, 1969). Surface settlement S(y) = Smax * exp(-y^2 / (2 * i^2)), where y is horizontal distance from tunnel centerline, i is trough width parameter (i = K * z0, K depends on soil type: 0.25 to 0.35 in sand, 0.4 to 0.6 in clay, z0 is tunnel axis depth). Volume loss Vs = sqrt(2*pi) * Smax * i. Target volume loss depends on TBM type and ground: 0.5 to 1.0% for well-controlled EPB in clay, 1 to 2% in sand.

Assess building damage from predicted settlement. Calculate angular distortion (differential settlement between footings divided by span). Classify damage using Burland and Wroth framework: negligible (< 1/500), slight (1/500 to 1/200), moderate (1/200 to 1/50). For buildings in the influence zone, do building-specific assessment: greenfield settlement modified by building stiffness (relative stiffness method, Potts and Addenbrooke).

For critical structures, run 2D or 3D numerical analysis. FEM with appropriate constitutive model (Hardening Soil for sand, Soft Soil Creep for soft clay). Model the TBM process: face pressure, grout pressure, contraction around shield, weight of backup. Validate model against measured settlements from similar projects.

Design the monitoring array. Settlement pins on surface at 2 to 5 m spacing across the trough, extending to at least 2 to 3 times i from centerline. Inclinometers adjacent to sensitive structures (installed to below tunnel invert). Extensometers for multi-point subsurface settlement where surface pins are insufficient. Automated total stations for real-time monitoring of structures. Piezometers to track groundwater response.

Set trigger levels. Green: measured settlement within predicted range. Amber: settlement exceeding prediction by a defined margin (typically 120 to 150% of predicted, or angular distortion approaching damage threshold). Red: settlement indicating loss of face control or unexpected ground behavior. Define contingency actions for each level: amber triggers increased monitoring frequency and TBM parameter review; red triggers TBM stoppage, emergency grouting, and engineering review.

Plan compensation grouting for sensitive structures. Tube-a-manchette (TAM) installation from surface or shaft before TBM arrival. Grout injection during and after TBM passage to compensate for ground loss. Injection controlled by real-time monitoring of structure settlement. Fracture grouting in clay, permeation grouting in sand.

description: Design reinforced and post-tensioned concrete members from load determination through flexural, shear, and serviceability checks to durability specification.

steps.description: Determine the load path through a concrete structure and identify critical members and sections for design.

inputs.name: structural-layout
inputs.desc: Geometry, spans, supports, and intended load-carrying system

inputs.name: loading-requirements
inputs.desc: Dead, live, wind, seismic, thermal, and any special loads with applicable code

outputs.name: load-combinations
outputs.desc: Factored load combinations per applicable code (ACI 318, Eurocode 2) with controlling combinations identified

outputs.name: critical-sections
outputs.desc: Member forces (M, V, N, T) at critical sections for each controlling load combination

process: Trace the gravity load path from slab to beam to column to foundation. Identify the lateral system: moment frame, shear wall, or dual system. Verify load path continuity (no load path discontinuities that create transfer structures without explicit design).
Calculate tributary areas for gravity members. For two-way slabs, use yield line or equivalent frame method for load distribution to beams. For one-way slabs, tributary width to supporting beams.

Apply load factors per code. ACI 318: 1.2D + 1.6L, 1.2D + 1.0W + 1.0L, 0.9D + 1.0W, 1.2D + 1.0E + 1.0L. Eurocode: 1.35G + 1.5Q, 1.35G + 1.5Q + 0.6*1.5W. Generate all required combinations and identify which controls at each section.

Run structural analysis. For regular frames: moment distribution or stiffness method. For complex structures: FEM (plate elements for slabs, beam elements for frames). For seismic: modal response spectrum analysis or equivalent lateral force. Extract M, V, N at critical sections: face of support for moment, d from face for shear, mid-span for deflection.
Identify sections requiring special attention: transfer beams, coupling beams, deep beams (span/depth < 4), corbels, beam-column joints, regions with high shear or torsion.

steps.description: Size reinforcement for flexural members using ultimate strength design with Whitney stress block.

inputs.name: critical-sections
inputs.desc: Factored moment, axial force at each section

inputs.name: structural-layout
inputs.desc: Member dimensions and material properties

outputs.name: flexural-reinforcement
outputs.desc: Required reinforcement area and layout at each critical section, with capacity check

outputs.name: ductility-verification
outputs.desc: Neutral axis depth ratio (c/d) and strain in tension steel confirming ductile behavior

process: Set material properties. f'c typically 28 to 55 MPa for normal construction. fy = 420 MPa (Grade 60) or 500 MPa (Eurocode). Effective depth d = h minus cover minus stirrup diameter minus half bar diameter.

Calculate required reinforcement from Mu. Using Whitney stress block: a = d - sqrt(d^2 - 2*Mu/(phi*0.85*f'c*b)), where phi = 0.9 for tension-controlled. Required As = 0.85*f'c*b*a/fy. Alternatively, use the resistance coefficient: Rn = Mu/(phi*b*d^2), then rho = (0.85*f'c/fy)*(1 - sqrt(1 - 2*Rn/(0.85*f'c))).

Check ductility. Verify c/d < 0.375 for tension-controlled behavior (epsilon_t > 0.005). If compression-controlled, increase section size or add compression steel. Check minimum reinforcement: As_min = max(3*sqrt(f'c)/fy * b*d, 200/fy * b*d) per ACI.

For doubly-reinforced sections: calculate moment capacity of tension steel alone. If insufficient, add compression steel. Compression steel contribution: As' = (Mu - phi*Mn_single)/(phi*fy*(d-d')). Verify compression steel yields: check strain compatibility at compression steel location.

Detail the reinforcement. Bar spacing must accommodate concrete placement (minimum clear spacing = max of bar diameter, 25 mm, 4/3 * aggregate size). Development length from ACI 318 Chapter 25. Curtailment: extend bars past theoretical cutoff by d or 12db. Lap splices in low-stress zones only.

steps.description: Design shear reinforcement and check torsion resistance using strut-and-tie where applicable.

inputs.name: critical-sections
inputs.desc: Factored shear and torsion at critical sections

inputs.name: flexural-reinforcement
inputs.desc: Longitudinal reinforcement layout already determined

outputs.name: shear-reinforcement
outputs.desc: Stirrup size, spacing, and extent for each member

outputs.name: torsion-reinforcement
outputs.desc: Closed stirrups and additional longitudinal steel for members subject to torsion

process: Calculate concrete shear contribution Vc. ACI simplified: Vc = 2*sqrt(f'c)*b*d (in psi units) or 0.17*sqrt(f'c)*b*d (in MPa). Detailed formula accounts for longitudinal reinforcement ratio and Mu/Vu*d ratio. For members with axial compression, Vc increases; with tension, Vc decreases.

Check if shear reinforcement is required: Vu > phi*Vc/2. If Vu > phi*Vc, provide stirrups. Required Vs = Vu/phi - Vc. Stirrup spacing: s = Av*fy*d/Vs. Maximum spacing: d/2 when Vs < 4*sqrt(f'c)*b*d, d/4 when Vs exceeds that. Verify Vs < 8*sqrt(f'c)*b*d (upper limit; if exceeded, increase section size).

For torsion: check if Tu > phi*Tcr/4, where Tcr = 4*sqrt(f'c)*(Acp^2/pcp). If Tu > phi*Tcr, provide closed stirrups. Required At/s = Tu*tan(theta)/(phi*2*Ao*fy), where Ao = 0.85*Aoh. Additional longitudinal steel: Al = At/s * ph * cot^2(theta). Theta typically 45 degrees.

For deep beams (clear span / depth < 4): strut-and-tie model. Define nodes at load and support points. Define struts (compression) and ties (tension). Check strut capacity: fcu = 0.85*beta_s*f'c (beta_s = 0.75 for bottle-shaped struts with reinforcement, 0.60 without). Check node bearing stress. Design tie reinforcement.

Detail stirrups. Hook details: 135-degree hooks for closed stirrups (seismic) or 90-degree plus 6db extension. Extend stirrups through full member depth. In beam-column joints for seismic frames: joint shear check per ACI 352, transverse reinforcement within the joint.

steps.description: Check deflection and crack width under service loads to meet functional and durability requirements.

inputs.name: flexural-reinforcement
inputs.desc: As-designed reinforcement at each section

inputs.name: load-combinations
inputs.desc: Service-level load combinations

outputs.name: deflection-check
outputs.desc: Calculated immediate and long-term deflections vs. allowable (L/240, L/480, etc.)

outputs.name: crack-width-check
outputs.desc: Calculated crack width at tension face vs. allowable per exposure class

process: Calculate immediate deflection. Effective moment of inertia Ie from Branson's equation: Ie = (Mcr/Ma)^3 * Ig + (1-(Mcr/Ma)^3) * Icr, where Mcr = fr*Ig/yt, fr = 7.5*sqrt(f'c) psi. For continuous beams, use weighted average of Ie at midspan and supports.

Calculate long-term deflection. Multiply immediate deflection from sustained load by lambda = xi/(1+50*rho'), where xi = 2.0 for 5 years or more, 1.4 for 12 months, 1.0 for 3 months. Compare total deflection to limits: L/240 for floors supporting non-structural elements, L/480 if those elements are likely to be damaged.

Check crack width. ACI approach: spacing factor s = 540/fs - 2.5*cc for beams (fs = service steel stress, cc = clear cover). Eurocode approach: wk = sr,max * (epsilon_sm - epsilon_cm), where sr,max = 3.4*c + 0.425*k1*k2*phi/rho_eff. Allowable crack width: 0.3 mm for normal exposure, 0.2 mm for aggressive, per Eurocode 2.

For post-tensioned members: verify class U (uncracked), T (transition), or C (cracked) per ACI 318. Class U: tensile stress < 7.5*sqrt(f'c) at service. Class T: between 7.5 and 12*sqrt(f'c). Calculate effective prestress after all losses (elastic shortening, creep, shrinkage, relaxation, friction, anchorage seating).

If deflection or crack width is excessive: options are increase section depth, add compression steel (reduces long-term deflection multiplier), increase As (reduces crack spacing), or apply prestressing to counteract dead load deflection.

steps.description: Specify concrete mix, cover, and protection measures for the target service life and exposure conditions.

inputs.name: structural-layout
inputs.desc: Member locations and environmental exposure

inputs.name: crack-width-check
inputs.desc: Service load crack width at each section

outputs.name: durability-specification
outputs.desc: Concrete mix requirements (w/c, f'c, air entrainment, SCMs), cover depths, and protection measures for each exposure class

outputs.name: maintenance-plan
outputs.desc: Inspection intervals and anticipated maintenance for target service life

process: Classify exposure per ACI 318 Table 19.3.1 or Eurocode EN 206. Categories: carbonation (XC1-4), chloride from seawater (XS1-3), chloride from deicing (XD1-3), freeze-thaw (XF1-4), chemical attack (XA1-3). Each member face gets the worst applicable class.

Set maximum w/c ratio from exposure class. Typical: 0.45 for XS2/XD2, 0.40 for XS3/XD3. Set minimum f'c (often 35 to 45 MPa for marine/deicing exposure). Specify SCMs: fly ash (15-25%), slag (35-65%), or silica fume (5-10%) for chloride resistance. Air entrainment 4-7% for freeze-thaw (XF classes).

Set cover depth. ACI minimum: 40 mm for exposed to weather, 50 mm for soil/seawater. Eurocode: structural class adjusted cover from cmin table. For 100-year design life, add 10 mm to 50-year values. Consider construction tolerance (delta_c = 10 mm typically).

For aggressive environments, specify additional protection. Epoxy-coated rebar or stainless steel in splash zone. Concrete surface treatment (silane/siloxane sealer) for chloride exposure. Cathodic protection for submerged marine structures. Waterproofing membrane for below-grade structures.

Define quality control requirements. Concrete testing: slump/flow, air content, temperature at delivery. Strength: cylinders per ACI 301 (minimum 1 per 100 m3 or per day). Chloride content limit: 0.06% by mass of cite for prestressed, 0.15% for reinforced in wet conditions. Permeability test (RCPT or bulk diffusion) for high-durability specifications.

description: Plan, execute, and interpret a geotechnical investigation campaign from desk study through field testing to ground model and geotechnical baseline report.

steps.description: Compile existing information and develop preliminary ground model before field investigation.

inputs.name: site-location
inputs.desc: Project site location and extent

inputs.name: project-requirements
inputs.desc: Type of structure, loads, and construction method driving investigation needs

outputs.name: preliminary-ground-model
outputs.desc: Expected stratigraphy, hazards, and key geotechnical questions to answer

outputs.name: investigation-plan
outputs.desc: Borehole locations, depths, in-situ and lab testing program

process: Gather published geological maps (USGS/BGS), soil survey maps, previous site investigation reports from nearby projects, aerial photographs (historical for fill/excavation detection), and utility records.

Identify geological hazards: faults, landslide susceptibility, liquefaction potential (in seismic zones with loose saturated sand), expansive soils, karst (sinkholes in limestone), mine workings, contamination.
Develop preliminary ground model: expected soil/rock types, approximate layer thicknesses, likely groundwater regime. Identify key unknowns that the investigation must resolve.

Plan investigation. Borehole spacing: 15 to 40 m for buildings, 25 to 100 m for linear infrastructure. Depth: 1.5 times foundation width below founding level for shallow foundations, or to competent rock for piled foundations. Include at least one deep borehole to full depth of influence.

Select in-situ testing program by anticipated ground type and design needs. CPTu everywhere possible (continuous profiling). SPT in boreholes where CPT refusal occurs. Vane shear in soft clay. Pressuremeter in rock or stiff soil. Flat plate dilatometer for settlement prediction in sand.

steps.description: Execute the field investigation: drilling, sampling, in-situ testing, and groundwater characterization.

inputs.name: investigation-plan
inputs.desc: Borehole locations, depths, and testing program

inputs.name: preliminary-ground-model
inputs.desc: Expected conditions to guide real-time field decisions

outputs.name: field-data
outputs.desc: Borehole logs, CPT profiles, in-situ test results, groundwater observations, and samples for laboratory

outputs.name: field-observations
outputs.desc: Notable conditions encountered: unexpected layers, obstructions, artesian pressures, contamination indicators

process: Set up boreholes. Rotary drilling for general use. Cable percussion (shell and auger) in soft ground with better sample quality. Sonic drilling for contaminated sites (sealed samples, minimal waste). Diamond core drilling in rock (double or triple tube barrel for core recovery; target > 95% TCR in competent rock).

Collect samples. Undisturbed samples in cohesive soil: thin-wall Shelby tube (75 mm diameter, pushed not driven) or piston sampler in very soft clay. Disturbed samples in granular soil from SPT split spoon. Rock core: log RQD, discontinuity spacing, orientation, roughness, infilling (use ISRM descriptors).

Run CPTu. Calibrate cone before and after each sounding. Push rate 2 cm/s. Record qt (corrected cone resistance), fs (sleeve friction), u2 (pore pressure at shoulder). Dissipation tests at selected depths in clay (time to 50% dissipation gives coefficient of consolidation). Plot Ic (soil behavior type index) to classify layers.

Install groundwater monitoring. Standpipe piezometers at key depths (one above and one below each confining layer). Vibrating wire piezometers for rapid response in low-permeability soils. Allow equilibration time (days in sand, weeks in clay) before reading. Record initial water strike levels during drilling separately from equilibrium levels.

Adapt program in real time. If unexpected conditions are found (softer layers, higher water table, boulders, contamination), modify depths, add boreholes, or change testing. Document all deviations from plan and their justification.

steps.description: Execute the laboratory testing program on collected samples for classification, strength, and deformability.

inputs.name: field-data
inputs.desc: Samples collected from boreholes with their depths and soil descriptions

outputs.name: lab-results
outputs.desc: Classification, strength, consolidation, and permeability test results by depth and location

outputs.name: design-parameters
outputs.desc: Characteristic and design values for each geotechnical unit (undrained shear strength, effective stress parameters, stiffness, permeability)

process: Classification tests on every sample: natural moisture content, Atterberg limits (LL, PL, PI) for cohesive soils, particle size distribution for granular soils. Classify per USCS. Specific gravity where needed for void ratio calculations.

Strength tests. Undrained shear strength in clay: UU triaxial (quick, multiple per borehole), CU triaxial with pore pressure measurement (fewer, but gives effective stress parameters c' and phi'). Effective stress parameters in sand: CD triaxial or direct shear. For rock: UCS (5 per rock unit minimum), point load test for supplementary data, Brazilian tensile strength.

Consolidation tests. One-dimensional oedometer on representative samples from each compressible layer. Determine Cc (compression index), Cr (recompression index), preconsolidation pressure (sigma_p from Casagrande construction), and cv (coefficient of consolidation from root-time or log-time method). At least 3 tests per compressible stratum.

Permeability tests. Falling head or constant head in the lab for cohesive soils. Note that lab permeability may underestimate field permeability by 1 to 2 orders (fabric effects, macro features). Compare with field values from pumping tests or CPT dissipation-derived ch.

Derive design parameters. Plot all data by depth and stratum. Remove outliers with justification. Select characteristic values: mean minus half a standard deviation for typical geotechnical assessment, or apply statistical methods per Eurocode 7 (cautious estimate of the mean). Distinguish between drained and undrained parameters. Derive constrained modulus from oedometer for settlement, or use CPT correlation (M = alpha*qt where alpha depends on soil type).

steps.description: Interpret all investigation data into a final ground model, design parameters, and geotechnical baseline report.

inputs.name: field-data
inputs.desc: All field investigation results

inputs.name: design-parameters
inputs.desc: Laboratory-derived parameters by stratum

inputs.name: preliminary-ground-model
inputs.desc: Pre-investigation expectations for comparison

outputs.name: final-ground-model
outputs.desc: Interpreted stratigraphic model with design parameters, groundwater regime, and geotechnical hazards

outputs.name: geotechnical-baseline-report
outputs.desc: GBR for construction: anticipated ground conditions, baseline parameters for contractual risk allocation

process: Cross-correlate all data sources. Plot borehole logs alongside CPT profiles. Use CPT Ic classification to bridge between boreholes. Correlate SPT N-values with CPT qt for consistency check. Identify layers by engineering behavior, not just geological origin.

Build cross-sections. Longitudinal and transverse sections through the site showing interpreted layer boundaries. Contour surfaces of key interfaces (top of rock, top of bearing stratum, base of soft clay). Show groundwater levels with seasonal range if known.

Assign design parameters to each stratum. Tabulate characteristic values of: unit weight, undrained shear strength (or friction angle and cohesion for drained), compression index, permeability, and stiffness. Provide ranges and recommended values. Note any spatial trends (increasing strength with depth in a clay unit).

Write the geotechnical baseline report (GBR) if for tunneling or complex construction. The GBR states the baseline conditions that the contractor prices against. Quantify: percentage of each ground type along alignment, groundwater inflows, abrasivity values for cutter life, boulders or obstructions, and any ground treatment required. Deviations from baseline during construction trigger contractual mechanisms.

Identify residual risks and recommend further investigation if needed. Flag areas where borehole spacing is wider than ideal, where unexpected conditions were found, or where parameter scatter is high. Provide recommendations for construction monitoring to verify design assumptions.

description: Design a bridge from type selection through structural analysis, girder and substructure design, bearings, seismic provisions, to inspection and load rating methodology.

steps.description: Select the optimal bridge type based on span, site conditions, constructability, and cost.

inputs.name: crossing-requirements
inputs.desc: Required clear spans, vertical clearances, roadway width, design speed, and loading

inputs.name: site-conditions
inputs.desc: Foundation conditions, navigational clearance, environmental constraints, access for construction

outputs.name: selected-bridge-type
outputs.desc: Bridge type with span arrangement, structural system, material, and construction method

outputs.name: preliminary-dimensions
outputs.desc: Approximate girder depths, pier heights, and foundation types

process: Match span range to bridge type. Up to 12 m: precast slab or box culvert. 12 to 40 m: precast prestressed girders (I, bulb-T, or box). 40 to 80 m: steel plate girders, segmental concrete box, or post-tensioned cast-in-place. 80 to 250 m: cable-stayed. Above 250 m to 2000 m: suspension. These ranges overlap; economy depends on local construction capability and material costs.

Select girder depth from span-to-depth ratios. Steel composite: L/25 for simple span, L/30 for continuous. Prestressed concrete: L/18 to L/22. Post-tensioned box: L/18 simple, L/20 to L/22 continuous. Cable-stayed: L/45 to L/60 for main span. These set preliminary section sizes for cost comparison.

Evaluate construction methods. Precast: crane erection (limited by crane reach and capacity, typically up to 60 to 80 ton girders), launched girders for viaducts. Segmental: balanced cantilever (no falsework below), span-by-span erection. Steel: erection by crane or launched. Site access and traffic staging often drive the choice more than structural efficiency.

Assess foundation requirements. Spread footings in rock or dense soil. Driven piles in soft ground (H-piles, pipe piles, precast concrete). Drilled shafts for high loads or hard driving conditions. Estimate foundation costs for each bridge type option.

Compare alternatives. Construct a cost comparison matrix: superstructure material and fabrication, erection, substructure, foundations, bearings and joints, maintenance over 75-year design life. Include non-cost factors: aesthetics (community input), constructability, schedule, environmental impact, resilience. Select the type with lowest life-cycle cost meeting all constraints.

steps.description: Perform structural analysis of the selected bridge type for all load combinations per AASHTO LRFD or applicable code.

inputs.name: selected-bridge-type
inputs.desc: Bridge type, span arrangement, and section properties

inputs.name: crossing-requirements
inputs.desc: Design loading (HL-93 or other), lane configuration

outputs.name: member-forces
outputs.desc: Enveloped moment, shear, and axial force at all critical sections for Strength, Service, and Fatigue limit states

outputs.name: live-load-distribution
outputs.desc: Distribution factors for moment and shear by girder, or results of refined analysis

process: Model the structure. For typical girder bridges: line girder analysis with AASHTO LRFD distribution factors (Table 4.6.2.2). For curved, skewed (> 20 degrees), or unusual bridges: grillage or 3D FEM with shell/beam elements. For cable-stayed: staged construction analysis tracking cable forces as deck extends.

Apply HL-93 loading: design truck (72 kip, 32/32/8 kip axles at 14/14-30 ft spacing) combined with design lane load (0.64 kip/ft). Or design tandem (50 kip, two 25-kip axles at 4 ft) combined with lane load. Use whichever produces larger effect. For negative moment and pier reactions, apply 90% of two trucks plus 90% of lane load in same span.

Calculate live load distribution factors. For moment in interior girders: g = 0.06 + (S/14)^0.4 * (S/L)^0.3 * (Kg/(12*L*ts^3))^0.1 (AASHTO approximate, in US customary units). For exterior girders: lever rule or special cases. Verify against refined analysis for non-standard configurations.

Generate force envelopes. Move the live load across the bridge to find the maximum and minimum force at each section. Combine with dead load (DC: structural components; DW: wearing surface, utilities) using load factors: Strength I: 1.25DC + 1.50DW + 1.75(LL+IM), where IM = 33% dynamic load allowance.

Check Service and Fatigue limit states. Service I: 1.0(DC+DW) + 1.0(LL+IM) for concrete stress limits. Service III: 1.0DC + 1.0DW + 0.8(LL+IM) for tension in prestressed concrete. Fatigue I: 1.75 times single design truck at 30 ft fixed axle spacing for infinite fatigue life check.

steps.description: Design the bridge superstructure: girders, deck, and connections.

inputs.name: member-forces
inputs.desc: Design forces at all critical sections

inputs.name: selected-bridge-type
inputs.desc: Bridge type and preliminary dimensions

outputs.name: superstructure-design
outputs.desc: Girder sections, deck reinforcement, shear connectors, diaphragms, and cross-frames

outputs.name: superstructure-drawings-data
outputs.desc: Key dimensions and reinforcement schedules for drafting

process: For steel composite girders: select plate sizes for flanges and web. Flange area from Mu/(phi*Fy*d_eff). Web depth from span-to-depth ratio, web thickness from shear and web buckling (compact, noncompact, or slender classification). Check all limit states: flexure (plastic moment or yield moment depending on section class), shear (end panels, interior panels with tension field action), fatigue at detail categories (welded stiffeners, coverplates, shear connectors).

For prestressed concrete girders: select strand pattern for required prestress force. Initial prestress force from service load conditions: at transfer, concrete stress at bottom fiber < 0.60*f'ci, at top fiber tension < 3*sqrt(f'ci). At service: bottom tension < 6*sqrt(f'c) for Class U (uncracked). Verify ultimate flexural capacity Mn > 1.2*Mcr to ensure ductile failure. Check shear using modified compression field theory (AASHTO Section 5).

Design the deck slab. Empirical design method if conditions are met (4 girders, no skew > 25 degrees, S < 4.1 m): minimum 175 mm top mat, 175 mm bottom mat isotropic reinforcement. Otherwise, strip method: 1-foot wide strip, design for HL-93 wheel load with dynamic allowance, one-way slab between girders.

Design shear connectors for composite action. Stud shear connectors: fatigue-controlled (number per unit length from Vsr*I/(Q*Zr) where Zr is allowable fatigue range per stud). Check ultimate capacity: total studs between zero and max moment must provide at least the lesser of 0.85*f'c*b_eff*ts or As*Fy.

Design cross-frames and diaphragms. Intermediate cross-frames at spacing not exceeding 7.5 m (AASHTO). End diaphragms for load distribution at bearings. K-frame or X-frame configuration. Check for wind and construction (wet concrete) load paths.

steps.description: Design bridge piers, abutments, and foundations for all loading including seismic.

inputs.name: member-forces
inputs.desc: Superstructure reactions at bearing locations

inputs.name: site-conditions
inputs.desc: Foundation soil/rock properties and seismic hazard

outputs.name: substructure-design
outputs.desc: Pier cap, columns, abutment walls, and wing walls with reinforcement

outputs.name: foundation-design
outputs.desc: Foundation type, size, depth, and reinforcement with bearing capacity and settlement checks

process: Design pier caps. Multi-column piers: inverted-T or rectangular cap beam. Straddle bents for wide crossings. Cap width sufficient for bearing seats with edge distance. Design for combined bending and shear from girder reactions. Check punching shear at concentrated load points.

Design pier columns. Slenderness check: if kl/r > 22, include second-order effects (moment magnification or P-delta analysis). Interaction diagram design: plot (Pu, Mu) for all load combinations and verify points are inside the interaction curve. Minimum reinforcement 1% of Ag, maximum 8% (but 4% practical limit for constructability). Confinement reinforcement per seismic zone.

Design abutments. Cantilever retaining wall type or integral abutment (eliminates expansion joints). For conventional: active earth pressure on stem (Ka * gamma * H * cos(delta)), at-rest if rigidly connected to deck. Check sliding (Fresist/Fslide > 1.5), overturning (Mr/Mo > 2.0 for service), and bearing pressure. Include live load surcharge equivalent to 0.6 m of soil behind wall.

Design foundations. Spread footings: bearing capacity from Terzaghi or Meyerhof (include shape, depth, inclination factors). Driven piles: static capacity from alpha method (clay) or beta method (sand), or from CPT direct methods (Eslami-Fellenius, LCPC). Drilled shafts: side resistance and base resistance per FHWA GEC 10. Group effects: efficiency factor for closely spaced piles.

Seismic design of substructure. Determine seismic hazard (AASHTO maps for 1000-year return period). Classify site (Site Class A through F from Vs30). Calculate elastic seismic forces. For SDC B, C: force-based design with R factors. For SDC D: displacement-based design using pushover analysis. Detail plastic hinges in columns with confining reinforcement to achieve target drift capacity.

steps.description: Select bearings and expansion joints, and establish the inspection and load rating methodology for the completed bridge.

inputs.name: superstructure-design
inputs.desc: Superstructure movements (thermal, creep, shrinkage, seismic) and reactions

inputs.name: substructure-design
inputs.desc: Substructure configurations and pier stiffness

outputs.name: bearings-and-joints
outputs.desc: Bearing type, size, and installation requirements; expansion joint type and movement range

outputs.name: inspection-and-rating-plan
outputs.desc: Inspection schedule, access requirements, element-level inspection items, and load rating methodology

process: Calculate bearing movements. Thermal: coefficient of expansion * temperature range * expansion length (from fixed point to bearing). Creep and shrinkage for concrete superstructures per AASHTO or CEB-FIP. Seismic displacement from analysis. Total movement is the algebraic sum of all sources.

Select bearing type. Elastomeric pads: for movements up to 50 mm and moderate rotations (simple span precast girders). PTFE sliding bearings: for large translations. Pot bearings or disc bearings: for high loads with rotation. Seismic isolation bearings (lead-rubber or friction pendulum): for SDC C/D to reduce seismic forces. Size elastomeric bearings: total elastomer thickness > 2 times maximum shear deformation; check shape factor (loaded area per free-to-bulge area) for compressive capacity.

Select expansion joints. Strip seals for movements up to 80 mm. Modular joints for larger movements (up to 600 mm). Finger joints for very large movements. Integral abutments eliminate joints entirely (suitable for total bridge length up to 90 m steel, 180 m concrete). Joint selection affects maintenance costs: joints and bearings are the highest-maintenance bridge components.

Establish inspection program per NBIS (National Bridge Inspection Standards). Routine inspection every 24 months. Fracture-critical inspection for non-redundant steel members annually. Underwater inspection every 60 months for submerged elements. Element-level inspection per AASHTO bridge element manual: rate each element condition state CS1 through CS4.

Develop load rating methodology. Inventory rating: HL-93 loading, phi factors per LRFR. Operating rating: higher capacity reflecting maximum permissible load. Rate all critical sections: positive and negative moment, shear at supports, connections, bearing capacity. Permit load analysis for overweight vehicles. If rating factor < 1.0: posting required or strengthening needed.

description: Design structures to resist earthquake forces: from seismic hazard analysis through system selection, analysis, detailing for ductility, to performance-based assessment.

steps.description: Determine the seismic hazard at the site and characterize site-specific ground motion.

inputs.name: site-location
inputs.desc: Geographic coordinates of the project site

inputs.name: site-geotechnical-data
inputs.desc: Shear wave velocity profile (Vs30 at minimum), soil stratigraphy

outputs.name: design-spectrum
outputs.desc: Site-specific design response spectrum (Sds, Sd1) and seismic design category

outputs.name: ground-motion-parameters
outputs.desc: PGA, spectral accelerations at key periods, and selected ground motion records if needed

process: Determine spectral acceleration parameters from USGS seismic hazard maps (or equivalent national maps). For ASCE 7: Ss (0.2s) and S1 (1.0s) for risk-targeted MCE (2% in 50 years, adjusted for risk). For Eurocode 8: ag from national annex zonation map for 475-year return period.

Classify site condition from Vs30. ASCE 7 Site Class: A (Vs30 > 1500 m/s hard rock), B (760-1500), C (360-760 dense soil/soft rock), D (180-360 stiff soil), E (< 180 soft soil), F (requires site-specific analysis: liquefiable soil, > 3 m peat, > 8 m soft clay with PI > 20 and su < 24 kPa).

Apply site coefficients. Fa (short period) and Fv (long period) from site class and mapped spectral values. Design spectrum: Sds = 2/3 * Fa * Ss, Sd1 = 2/3 * Fv * S1. Construct the design spectrum: plateau at Sds from T=0 to T=Sd1/Sds, then 1/T decay.

Determine Seismic Design Category from Sds, Sd1, and risk category. SDC A: no seismic design. SDC B: basic detailing. SDC C: intermediate detailing. SDC D/E/F: special detailing required, non-linear analysis may be needed.

For Site Class F or when site-specific analysis is required: run 1D equivalent-linear (SHAKE) or nonlinear site response analysis. Input: shear wave velocity profile, modulus reduction and damping curves, bedrock ground motions. Check for liquefaction potential: factor of safety from SPT or CPT-based methods (Boulanger and Idriss 2014), assess post-liquefaction settlement and lateral spread.

steps.description: Select the lateral force-resisting system and configure the structure for seismic performance.

inputs.name: design-spectrum
inputs.desc: Site-specific design spectrum and seismic design category

inputs.name: structural-layout
inputs.desc: Building plan dimensions, height, occupancy, and architectural constraints

outputs.name: lateral-system
outputs.desc: Selected LFRS type, R factor, redundancy factor, and system configuration

outputs.name: seismic-weight
outputs.desc: Effective seismic weight and mass distribution by floor

process: Select LFRS type based on SDC, height, and performance objectives. Steel special moment frames: high ductility (R=8), no height limit, flexible (large drifts, expensive connections). Steel special concentrically braced frames: moderate ductility (R=6), good stiffness, limited height in SDC D/E. Steel eccentrically braced frames: R=8, combines stiffness and ductility. Reinforced concrete special moment frames: R=8, no height limit. RC special shear walls: R=5-6, excellent stiffness, most economical for mid-rise. Dual systems: combine frame and walls for redundancy.

Configure the system in plan. Provide lateral resistance in both orthogonal directions. Minimize eccentricity between center of mass and center of rigidity to limit torsion. Irregularity checks: torsional irregularity if max drift > 1.2 times average drift. Soft story if stiffness < 70% of story above. Avoid re-entrant corners > 15% of plan dimension, or provide collector elements.

Configure vertically. Avoid soft stories (reduce stiffness discontinuity). Avoid weak stories (strength discontinuity). Weight irregularity if any story mass > 150% of adjacent story. Vertical geometric irregularity if lateral system dimension changes > 130%. These irregularities trigger more stringent analysis requirements.

Calculate seismic weight. Include full dead load plus applicable portion of live load (25% of floor live in storage and warehouse, 20% of flat roof snow > 30 psf, full weight of permanent equipment). Distribute to each floor. Calculate effective modal mass for each mode.

Check system compatibility with architectural requirements. Moment frame bay widths must align with architectural grid. Braced frame locations must avoid doorways and windows. Shear wall locations must be architecturally acceptable and have adequate foundations. Resolve conflicts before proceeding to analysis.

steps.description: Perform seismic analysis using the appropriate method for the structure's characteristics and SDC.

inputs.name: lateral-system
inputs.desc: Selected LFRS, R factor, configuration

inputs.name: design-spectrum
inputs.desc: Design response spectrum and ground motion records

inputs.name: seismic-weight
inputs.desc: Mass distribution by floor

outputs.name: seismic-forces
outputs.desc: Design base shear, story forces, story drifts, and member forces for each load combination

outputs.name: drift-check
outputs.desc: Interstory drift ratios vs. allowable limits at each story

process: Equivalent Lateral Force (ELF) method for regular structures in SDC B/C. Base shear V = Cs * W, where Cs = Sds/(R/Ie) but not less than 0.044*Sds*Ie or 0.01 (and not less than 0.5*S1/(R/Ie) where S1 >= 0.6g). Distribute vertically: Fx = Cvx * V, where Cvx = wx*hx^k / sum(wi*hi^k), k=1 for T<=0.5s, k=2 for T>=2.5s, interpolate between.

Modal Response Spectrum Analysis for irregular structures or when required by SDC. Build analytical model (centerline or with rigid end offsets). Run eigenvalue analysis to get periods and mode shapes. Include enough modes to capture 90% of total mass in each direction. Apply design spectrum to each mode, combine with CQC (Complete Quadratic Combination). Scale results so base shear >= 100% of ELF base shear (ASCE 7-22) or 85% (ASCE 7-16).

Nonlinear Response History Analysis for complex or high-importance structures. Select minimum 11 ground motion pairs (7 per ASCE 7-16). Scale to match design spectrum over period range 0.2T to 2.0T. Run time-history analysis with appropriate hysteretic models. Use mean of 11 results for design (maximum of 7 for ASCE 7-16). Check acceptance criteria: drift, plastic rotation, force demands in force-controlled elements.

Check interstory drift. Amplify elastic drift by Cd/Ie. Allowable: 0.020*hsx for most buildings, 0.010*hsx for masonry, 0.025*hsx for single-story steel. Drift often controls the design for moment frames (push toward larger sections or add stiffness). P-delta check: stability coefficient theta = Px*delta/(Vx*hsx*Cd) < 0.10 without further analysis.

Combine seismic with gravity loads. Basic combination: 1.2D + 1.0E + 1.0L + 0.2S, where E = rho*QE + 0.2*Sds*D (vertical seismic). Also check 0.9D - 0.2*Sds*D + rho*QE for overturning and uplift. Apply orthogonal combination: 100% in one direction + 30% in orthogonal direction.

steps.description: Detail structural members to achieve the ductility capacity assumed by the R factor in design.

inputs.name: seismic-forces
inputs.desc: Design forces from seismic analysis

inputs.name: lateral-system
inputs.desc: LFRS type and R factor

outputs.name: seismic-detailing
outputs.desc: Connection details, confinement reinforcement, capacity-protected elements, and plastic hinge regions

outputs.name: capacity-design-checks
outputs.desc: Verification of strong-column/weak-beam, overstrength at connections, and non-ductile failure prevention

process: Apply capacity design philosophy. Identify intended plastic hinge locations (beam ends in moment frames, link beams in EBF, wall base). Design these locations for the code-required ductility. Design all other elements (columns, connections, foundations) for the overstrength capacity of the plastic hinges, not the code design forces.

For RC special moment frames: strong column / weak beam requirement (sum of Mnc >= 1.2 * sum of Mnb at each joint). Confine plastic hinge regions in beams: hoops at s = min(d/4, 6db, 150 mm) over 2h from face of column. Confine columns: spiral or hoops over lo = max(h, L/6, 450 mm) from each end, with Ash calculated to maintain axial capacity after cover spalling. Joint shear: Vn = gamma*sqrt(f'c)*Aj where gamma depends on confinement.

For steel special moment frames: prequalified connections (per AISC 358) that can develop 0.04 radian plastic rotation. Reduced beam section (RBS, 'dogbone') is most common. Panel zone design: allow limited yielding in panel zone but avoid excessive deformation. Lateral bracing of beam flanges at plastic hinge locations. Column splices: full penetration welds or slip-critical bolted, located away from potential plastic hinges.

For RC special shear walls: boundary elements where maximum compressive strain exceeds 0.003 (check neutral axis depth at Mn). Confine boundary elements over depth of neutral axis and extend vertically above and below the critical section. Shear design: Vn = Acv*(alpha_c*sqrt(f'c) + rho_t*fy), where alpha_c = 3 for hw/lw >= 2.0, 2 for hw/lw <= 1.5. Web reinforcement in two directions, minimum rho = 0.0025.

For steel braced frames: ensure brace connections can develop expected brace capacity (Ry*Fy*Ag in tension, 1.14*Fy*Ag for overstrength). Gusset plate design: Whitmore section for tension, Thornton method for compression (buckling of gusset). Balanced design: columns designed for mechanism-level forces. For BRB (buckling-restrained brace): verify qualification testing per AISC 341 (2% story drift, cumulative ductility 200).

steps.description: Evaluate structural performance against multiple hazard levels using ASCE 41 or equivalent for existing or high-importance structures.

inputs.name: seismic-detailing
inputs.desc: As-designed or as-built structural details

inputs.name: ground-motion-parameters
inputs.desc: Ground motions for multiple hazard levels (serviceability, design, MCE)

outputs.name: performance-assessment
outputs.desc: Structural performance level achieved at each hazard level (IO, LS, CP) with component-level acceptance checks

outputs.name: retrofit-recommendations
outputs.desc: If existing structure: identified deficiencies and recommended retrofit measures

process: Define performance objectives. ASCE 41 basic performance objective for existing buildings (BPOE): Life Safety at BSE-1E (225-year), Collapse Prevention at BSE-2E (975-year). For new buildings seeking enhanced performance: Immediate Occupancy at design earthquake, or Operational at serviceability earthquake.

Classify components as deformation-controlled or force-controlled. Deformation-controlled: members that can sustain inelastic deformation (beams in flexure, brace in tension). Force-controlled: brittle failure modes (shear in columns, connection fracture). For deformation-controlled: compare demand to m-factor modified capacity (linear) or to plastic rotation limits (nonlinear). For force-controlled: compare demand to lower-bound capacity with QUF <= phi*QCL.

Linear analysis: static or dynamic. Calculate demand-to-capacity ratios (DCR). For deformation-controlled: DCR = QUD / (m * QCE * kappa). If DCR > 1.0, the element does not meet the performance level. The m-factor depends on element type, detail category, and performance level (from ASCE 41 tables). For force-controlled: QUF = QG + QE/(C1*C2*J).

Nonlinear analysis: pushover (static) or response history (dynamic). Pushover: apply lateral forces proportional to first mode shape, push to target displacement (ASCE 41 coefficient method: delta_t = C0*C1*C2*Sa*Te^2/(4*pi^2)). Plot base shear vs. roof displacement. Check plastic rotation at each hinge against acceptance criteria. Response history: more accurate for irregular structures or when higher modes are significant.

For existing buildings requiring retrofit: identify deficiencies (columns with insufficient confinement, inadequate connections, soft stories, torsion). Select retrofit measures: FRP wrapping for column confinement, steel jacketing, addition of shear walls or braced frames, base isolation for entire building, supplemental damping (viscous dampers, friction dampers). Re-analyze retrofitted structure to verify performance objectives are met.

description: Design a high-speed transport system: guideway alignment, propulsion, levitation, tube environment, stations, and energy analysis.

steps.description: Design the horizontal and vertical alignment of the guideway for target speed and passenger comfort.

inputs.name: route-endpoints
inputs.desc: Origin and destination with intermediate stop requirements

inputs.name: design-speed
inputs.desc: Maximum operating speed and vehicle characteristics

outputs.name: alignment-geometry
outputs.desc: Horizontal curves (radius, superelevation, transition lengths), vertical grades, and station locations

outputs.name: right-of-way-requirements
outputs.desc: Corridor width, property acquisition needs, utility conflicts

process: Set minimum horizontal curve radius from speed, superelevation, and comfort. R = V^2 / (g * (e + f)), where V is speed, e is superelevation (bank angle), f is unbalanced lateral acceleration limit. For passenger comfort: unbalanced acceleration < 0.05g for seated passengers. For 300 km/h with 8 degrees cant: R approximately 4,200 m. For 1,000 km/h in a tube at 15 degrees: R approximately 25,000 m.

Design transition curves between tangent and circular curves. Clothoid (Euler spiral) for gradual introduction of curvature and superelevation. Length of transition: roll rate for superelevation change limited to 5 degrees/s for conventional, possibly higher for enclosed pods. At high speeds, transitions are several kilometers long.

Set vertical alignment. Maximum grade depends on propulsion capability at speed. Maglev: up to 8 to 10%. Wheel-on-rail HSR: up to 3.5 to 4%. Vertical curves: minimum radius from vertical acceleration limit (0.3 m/s2 for comfort on crests). Crest curve radius R = V^2 / (3.6^2 * a_v). At 300 km/h: R approximately 23,000 m.

Locate stations for passenger access and system operations. Stations at population centers and transport hubs. Deceleration distance from maximum speed: several km depending on comfortable deceleration (1.0 to 1.5 m/s2 for seated passengers). Include bypass tracks at stations for non-stop services if applicable.

Define right-of-way. Guideway structure width plus clearance envelope plus maintenance access plus safety setback. For elevated guideway: typically 15 to 25 m corridor. For tunnel: surface easement width depends on depth. Identify utility relocations, road crossings, and environmental sensitive areas requiring avoidance or mitigation.

steps.description: Select and size the propulsion and levitation systems for the target speed and vehicle mass.

inputs.name: design-speed
inputs.desc: Maximum operating speed, acceleration, and braking requirements

inputs.name: alignment-geometry
inputs.desc: Grades, curves, and station spacing affecting propulsion loads

outputs.name: propulsion-specification
outputs.desc: Propulsion technology, power rating, force-speed curve, and wayside/onboard split

outputs.name: levitation-specification
outputs.desc: Levitation technology, air gap, weight capacity, guidance system, and power requirements

process: Decompose drag forces at design speed. Aerodynamic drag: Fd = 0.5 * rho * Cd * A * V^2. In open air at 300 km/h, this dominates. In a tube at reduced pressure (100 Pa), drag drops proportionally but Kantrowitz limit creates choke effects that increase drag if tube diameter is too small relative to pod diameter (blockage ratio). Magnetic drag for maglev: significant at low speed, decreasing with speed. Mechanical drag (rolling resistance if wheel-on-rail): Fr = mu * m * g, where mu approximately 0.002 for steel wheel on rail.

Select propulsion technology. Linear induction motor (LIM): simpler, lower cost, lower efficiency at high speed (end effects, large air gap losses). Linear synchronous motor (LSM): higher efficiency (> 90%), precise speed control, but requires powered track (higher infrastructure cost). For very high speed (> 500 km/h): LSM preferred for efficiency. Permanent magnet LSM (PM-LSM) for highest efficiency.

Size propulsion. Required thrust at maximum speed equals total drag at that speed plus grade resistance component. Power = thrust * velocity. Acceleration thrust: F = m * a + drag(v) + grade(v), integrated over the speed range from zero to max. Total installed power from the acceleration profile. Wayside power supply sizing: peak power from multiple vehicles accelerating simultaneously, regeneration from braking vehicles.

Select levitation technology. Electromagnetic suspension (EMS): attractive force, inherently unstable (requires active gap control at kHz bandwidth), small gap (8-12 mm), works at zero speed (no minimum levitation speed). Electrodynamic suspension (EDS): repulsive force from induced currents, inherently stable but requires minimum speed (5-10 km/h for superconducting magnets), larger gap (100-150 mm), needs wheels for low speed. Passive permanent magnet Halbach arrays: lighter, no power draw, but limited gap and load capacity.

Design the guidance system. Lateral guidance from dedicated magnets (separate from levitation) or combined levitation-guidance configuration. For EMS: guidance magnets on side rails. For EDS: null-flux figure-8 coils provide combined lift and guidance. Guidance force must exceed worst-case lateral loads: crosswind on exposed guideway, curve negotiation, switch passing. Backup mechanical guidance (skids) for fault conditions.

steps.description: Design the tube or tunnel environment: pressure management, emergency ventilation, evacuation, and thermal control.

inputs.name: alignment-geometry
inputs.desc: Tube/tunnel length, cross-section, and portal locations

inputs.name: propulsion-specification
inputs.desc: Vehicle speed, heat rejection, and air displacement

outputs.name: tube-environment-design
outputs.desc: Pressure level, pumping system, thermal management, and ventilation for normal and emergency operations

outputs.name: emergency-egress-plan
outputs.desc: Evacuation routes, refuge areas, ventilation for fire scenarios, and rescue access points

process: For reduced-pressure tube systems: determine target pressure from drag analysis. Lower pressure reduces aerodynamic drag but increases pumping cost and leak management complexity. Typical target: 100 to 1000 Pa. Calculate pumping capacity: initial pumpdown volume, steady-state leak rate from joints and airlocks, air displaced by vehicle entry/exit through airlocks.

For conventional high-speed rail in tunnel: manage pressure waves from train entry and passage. Piston effect: train entering tunnel compresses air ahead. Micro-pressure waves emitted from tunnel exit (tunnel boom). Mitigation: enlarge tunnel cross-section (blockage ratio < 0.12 for single track), add pressure relief shafts, or install hood structures at portals to slow compression.

Thermal management. Heat sources: propulsion losses, braking energy, passenger metabolic heat, solar gain on exposed guideway. In a sealed tube, heat accumulates without active removal. Design heat rejection: ventilation shafts at intervals, heat exchangers along tube wall, or circulating coolant in guideway structure. Calculate thermal equilibrium: steady-state temperature rise must stay within equipment and comfort limits.

Emergency ventilation for fire scenarios. Design to tenable conditions: visibility > 10 m, temperature < 60 C, CO < 1000 ppm at head height along egress route. Longitudinal ventilation: jet fans or mechanical ventilation to push smoke in one direction, passengers evacuate in the other. Critical velocity to prevent backlayering: Vc = Kp * (g * H * Q / (rho * cp * T * A))^(1/3) where Q is fire heat release rate.

Design evacuation. Maximum distance between emergency exits: 250 m for rail tunnels (NFPA 502), may be shorter for other transport types. Cross-passages between twin-bore tunnels every 250 m. Refuge areas with fresh air supply and communication at intervals. Emergency lighting and wayfinding. Emergency walkway alongside guideway: minimum 1.2 m wide, non-slip, with handrail. Rescue train or vehicle access for injured persons.

steps.description: Design stations for high-speed transport: platform operations, passenger flow, and interface with local transport.

inputs.name: alignment-geometry
inputs.desc: Station locations along alignment and approach geometry

inputs.name: tube-environment-design
inputs.desc: Pressure transition requirements at stations (for tube systems)

outputs.name: station-layout
outputs.desc: Platform configuration, passenger processing areas, airlock or pressure transition zones, vertical circulation

outputs.name: passenger-flow-model
outputs.desc: Design capacity, level of service at pinch points, dwell time, and headway

process: Determine platform configuration. Through-station (trains pass through) vs. terminal (trains reverse). Number of platforms from service frequency and dwell time: minimum 2 for bidirectional service with backup. Platform length from vehicle length. Platform screen doors for safety and environment control (mandatory for reduced-pressure systems, recommended for conventional HSR at > 200 km/h).

For tube systems: design airlock or pressure transition. Vehicle enters atmospheric-pressure station chamber, doors open, passengers board/alight, doors close, chamber depressurizes, vehicle departs into tube. Or continuous system where station is also at reduced pressure with airlocks for passenger access. Airlock cycle time directly affects system headway and capacity.

Model passenger flow. Level of service standards: LOS C or better for paid areas (1.0 to 1.5 m2/person). Stairway and escalator capacity: 4,500 to 6,000 persons/hour per meter width for stairs. Elevator capacity for accessibility: 10% of peak 15-minute passenger volume. Security screening throughput if required. Simulate peak 15-minute arrivals and departures using pedestrian microsimulation or Fruin analysis.

Design intermodal connections. Locate station for connection to metro, bus, taxi, and private vehicle. Kiss-and-ride and park-and-ride capacity from catchment analysis. Minimize transfer distance and level changes between modes. Wayfinding: clear sightlines to platforms from all entrances.

Calculate system capacity. Headway from signaling system minimum (for rail: moving block or fixed block) or airlock cycle time (for tube). Vehicles per hour per direction * passengers per vehicle = peak-hour passengers per direction (pphpd). Typical targets: 8,000 to 15,000 pphpd for high-speed rail, potentially lower for pod-based tube systems. Match capacity to demand forecast with growth margin.

steps.description: Analyze energy consumption, operating costs, and financial viability of the high-speed transport system.

inputs.name: propulsion-specification
inputs.desc: Propulsion power, efficiency, and energy recovery capability

inputs.name: passenger-flow-model
inputs.desc: Daily ridership, load factors, and service frequency

outputs.name: energy-analysis
outputs.desc: Energy consumption per passenger-km, annual energy cost, regeneration fraction, and comparison to competing modes

outputs.name: financial-model
outputs.desc: Capital cost, operating cost, revenue projection, and cost recovery timeline

process: Calculate energy per trip. Integrate propulsion power over the speed-distance profile: acceleration phase (high power), cruise (drag power), braking (regeneration). Energy = integral of (F_propulsion * v) dt. Subtract regenerated braking energy (typically 20 to 40% recovery for electric propulsion). Add hotel loads (HVAC, lighting, doors) and infrastructure loads (pumps, guideway systems, stations).

Express as energy per passenger-km. Divide trip energy by (seats * load factor * distance). Compare to competing modes: airline (1.5 to 3.0 MJ/pax-km), automobile (2.0 to 3.5 MJ/pax-km), conventional rail (0.3 to 0.8 MJ/pax-km). High-speed rail typically 0.3 to 0.6 MJ/pax-km. Reduced-pressure tube systems target below 0.2 MJ/pax-km due to low drag.

Calculate annual energy cost from annual service-km, energy per km, and electricity tariff. Consider time-of-use pricing: shift energy-intensive operations (tube pumping, pre-cooling) to off-peak. Solar PV along guideway: estimate generation from exposed area, local irradiance, and capacity factor. Net energy cost after self-generation.

Build capital cost estimate. Infrastructure: guideway or tunnel per km (heavily variable: $50M to $500M per km for tunnel, $30M to $80M per km for elevated). Vehicles: per unit. Systems: signaling, communications, power supply, station fit-out. Land acquisition. Contingency (30 to 50% for novel technology). Total capital cost for the project.

Build financial model. Revenue from ridership * fare. Operating cost: energy, maintenance (infrastructure and vehicles, typically 2 to 4% of capital per year), staff, insurance. Farebox recovery ratio target. Project finance structure: debt service coverage ratio (DSCR > 1.3 for bankability). Sensitivity analysis: ridership variation, cost overrun, interest rate. Benefit-cost ratio including travel time savings, emission reduction, accident avoidance.

description: Design a water treatment plant from raw water characterization through treatment train selection, process design, and regulatory compliance.

steps.description: Characterize raw water quality and quantity to establish design basis for treatment.

inputs.name: water-source
inputs.desc: Source type (river, lake, reservoir, groundwater) and location

inputs.name: demand-projection
inputs.desc: Peak and average daily demand, projected population and growth rate

outputs.name: raw-water-quality
outputs.desc: Seasonal water quality data: turbidity, color, TOC, alkalinity, hardness, pH, temperature, microbial, and regulated contaminants

outputs.name: design-flows
outputs.desc: Average day, maximum day, and peak hour design flows with future expansion allowance

process: Collect minimum 12 months of raw water quality data (monthly sampling, more frequent during events). Key parameters: turbidity (NTU), color (TCU), total organic carbon (TOC, mg/L), alkalinity and pH (for coagulation design), temperature (affects reaction rates), dissolved oxygen, iron, manganese, ammonia.

Test for regulated contaminants: total coliforms, E. coli, Cryptosporidium and Giardia (if surface water), disinfection byproduct precursors (THM and HAA formation potential), lead and copper (at distribution system), nitrate, arsenic, fluoride, PFAS (emerging contaminant).

Characterize seasonal variation. Turbidity spikes from runoff events (spring melt, storms). Algae blooms in summer (taste-and-odor compounds: geosmin, MIB). Low temperature in winter (affects coagulation kinetics, slower settling). Plot exceedance curves for key parameters to identify design conditions.

Calculate design flows. Average day demand from per-capita demand * population + industrial/commercial. Maximum day: average day * peaking factor (1.5 to 2.0 depending on climate and system characteristics). Peak hour: maximum day * hourly peaking factor (1.5 to 1.8). Include fire flow if treatment plant supplies it directly. Add 10 to 20% for future growth or system losses.

Assess treatability. Jar testing: vary coagulant dose and pH to find optimum for turbidity and organics removal. Settle for 30 minutes, filter through Whatman No. 1, measure residual turbidity, color, and TOC. Repeat at different raw water qualities (low turbidity, high turbidity, cold water). This data drives coagulant selection and dose range for design.

steps.description: Select the treatment process sequence based on raw water quality, regulatory requirements, and project constraints.

inputs.name: raw-water-quality
inputs.desc: Seasonal raw water data including contaminant profiles

inputs.name: design-flows
inputs.desc: Design flow rates for sizing

outputs.name: treatment-train
outputs.desc: Selected processes in sequence with design criteria for each unit

outputs.name: chemical-requirements
outputs.desc: Chemicals needed (coagulant, polymer, disinfectant, pH adjustment) with estimated dose ranges

process: Match contaminants to processes. Turbidity/particles: coagulation + flocculation + sedimentation + filtration (conventional treatment). Dissolved organics (TOC, color): enhanced coagulation (higher dose, lower pH) or activated carbon. Pathogens: filtration (Crypto/Giardia removal credit) plus disinfection (chlorine, UV, ozone). Iron/manganese: oxidation (aeration, chlorine, permanganate) followed by filtration. Hardness: lime softening. Taste and odor: powdered activated carbon or ozone.

Select coagulant. Aluminum sulfate (alum): effective pH range 5.5 to 7.5, well understood. Ferric chloride or ferric sulfate: wider pH range (4.5 to 9.0), better for cold water, lower residual aluminum. Polyaluminum chloride (PACl): faster floc formation, less sludge, performs better at low temperature. Polymer: cationic for charge neutralization, anionic/nonionic for floc building. Dose from jar test data.

Configure sedimentation. Conventional rectangular basins: surface overflow rate 1.0 to 2.5 m/h (40 to 100 m3/m2/d) for alum floc. Plate or tube settlers: higher rate (3 to 6 m/h) in less footprint. Dissolved air flotation (DAF): for low-turbidity, high-algae water (effective for light floc that does not settle well). Contact time typically 2 to 4 hours for conventional sedimentation.

Configure filtration. Rapid gravity filters: dual media (anthracite over sand) at 5 to 15 m/h. Filter depth: 600 mm anthracite, 300 mm sand. Backwash: air scour + water at 40 to 60 m/h, 15 to 20 minutes. Membrane filtration (microfiltration or ultrafiltration): absolute barrier for Crypto and Giardia (4-log removal credit), higher cost, lower chemical use. Select based on source water quality and log removal credit needed.

Configure disinfection. Primary disinfection: chlorine (CT concept: concentration * contact time for target log inactivation from CT tables. For 3-log Giardia at 10 C, pH 7: CT approximately 100 mg-min/L). UV: effective for Crypto (40 mJ/cm2 for 4-log), does not provide residual. Ozone: strong oxidant for taste-and-odor, Crypto inactivation, but forms bromate in high-bromide water. Secondary disinfection: chloramine for distribution system residual (lower DBP formation than free chlorine).

steps.description: Size and detail each unit process in the treatment train for the design flow.

inputs.name: treatment-train
inputs.desc: Selected processes with design criteria

inputs.name: design-flows
inputs.desc: Average and maximum day flows

outputs.name: process-sizing
outputs.desc: Dimensions, number of units, and equipment specifications for each process

outputs.name: hydraulic-profile
outputs.desc: Water surface elevations through the plant from intake to clearwell

process: Size rapid mix. Velocity gradient G = 300 to 1000 s^-1 for 10 to 60 seconds. Power required P = mu * G^2 * V, where mu is dynamic viscosity and V is chamber volume. Mechanical mixer or in-line static mixer. For in-line: select mixer diameter and number of elements for target G at design flow.

Size flocculation. Three-stage tapered flocculation: G = 60-80 s^-1 in first stage, 30-50 in second, 15-30 in third. Total detention time 20 to 40 minutes at maximum day flow. Paddle, turbine, or vertical turbine flocculators. Gt product (G * detention time) typically 20,000 to 200,000. Provide at least 2 parallel trains for redundancy.

Size sedimentation basins. Surface overflow rate at maximum day flow: 1.0 to 2.5 m/h (lower for cold water, higher with tube settlers). Length-to-width ratio 4:1 to 6:1 for rectangular basins. Weir loading rate < 250 m3/m/d. Sludge collection: chain-and-flight or suction header, sludge hopper at inlet end. Minimum 2 basins for maintenance flexibility.

Size filters. Filtration rate at maximum day flow with one filter out of service: 5 to 12 m/h. Number of filters from total area required: minimum 4, use formula N = 0.044*sqrt(Q) where Q is in m3/d for larger plants. Individual filter area: 50 to 150 m2 (limited by backwash capacity and media distribution). Underdrain system: Leopold blocks, nozzles, or gravel support with header-lateral. Provide backwash rate 40 to 60 m/h with air scour at 50 to 80 m/h.

Build hydraulic profile. Start from clearwell design water level and work upstream, adding head losses through each unit: filter (clean head loss 0.3 m, terminal 2.5 m), piping (Hazen-Williams or Darcy-Weisbach), flocculation chambers (0.1 to 0.3 m), sedimentation weirs, rapid mix. The intake must be high enough to gravity-feed the plant, or provide raw water pumping to overcome the head requirement.

steps.description: Establish regulatory compliance monitoring, residuals handling, and operational procedures.

inputs.name: process-sizing
inputs.desc: Designed treatment processes and their capabilities

inputs.name: chemical-requirements
inputs.desc: Chemical systems and expected dose ranges

outputs.name: compliance-monitoring-plan
outputs.desc: Monitoring schedule, parameters, locations, and reporting requirements per drinking water regulations

outputs.name: residuals-management
outputs.desc: Sludge quantities, treatment, and disposal method

process: Map regulatory requirements. US: Safe Drinking Water Act, EPA primary and secondary standards. Surface Water Treatment Rule: minimum 3-log Giardia, 4-log virus removal/inactivation. Disinfectants/DBP Rule: TTHM < 80 ug/L, HAA5 < 60 ug/L (Stage 2 DBPR). Lead and Copper Rule: action levels. State-specific requirements may be more stringent.

Design continuous monitoring. Turbidity: individual filter effluent turbidimeters (< 0.3 NTU in 95% of readings, never > 1 NTU for conventional). Combined filter effluent for compliance reporting. Chlorine residual: continuous analyzer at entry to distribution (free or total depending on disinfectant). pH, temperature at key process points. Flow measurement for CT calculation.

Design sampling program. Daily: turbidity, chlorine residual, pH. Monthly: coliform bacteria (total coliform rule: < 5% positive in distribution). Quarterly or annual (depending on system size): DBPs, inorganic chemicals, SOCs, VOCs, radionuclides. Establish sampling locations: raw water, settled water, filter effluent, clearwell, distribution system entry point, and distribution system sampling sites.

Estimate residuals. Sludge production from coagulation: 0.5 to 1.5 kg dry solids per m3 of water treated (depends on raw water turbidity and coagulant dose). Filter backwash water: 2 to 5% of plant production.
