Dewatering options: gravity thickening to 2 to 4% solids, then mechanical dewatering (belt filter press to 15 to 25%, centrifuge to 20 to 30%, or plate-and-frame press to 30 to 40%). Disposal: landfill (if passes TCLP for metals), land application, or sanitary sewer (check local limits).

Develop operating procedures. Startup sequence for each process unit. Chemical feed calibration procedure. Filter backwash initiation criteria (time, head loss, turbidity breakthrough). Emergency procedures: raw water quality event (increase coagulant, switch to backup source), filter breakthrough (take filter offline, investigate), loss of disinfection (boil water advisory protocol). Operator certification requirements per state.

description: Design deep foundations from pile type selection through capacity estimation, lateral load analysis, group effects, load testing, and integrity verification.

steps.description: Select the optimal pile type based on load requirements, ground conditions, and site constraints.

inputs.name: structural-loads
inputs.desc: Axial (compression, tension), lateral, and moment demands at foundation level

inputs.name: ground-conditions
inputs.desc: Soil/rock profile with strength, stiffness, and groundwater from geotechnical investigation

outputs.name: selected-pile-type
outputs.desc: Pile type, material, diameter/section, expected length, and installation method

outputs.name: pile-feasibility-assessment
outputs.desc: Constructability considerations: access, vibration limits, noise, nearby structures, spoil disposal

process: Match pile type to ground and load. Driven steel H-piles: good in mixed ground, can penetrate dense layers, easy to extend/cut, but cannot develop large base resistance in soil. Driven precast concrete: high axial capacity in bearing soils, displacement pile (densifies sand), limited by driving stresses. Driven steel pipe: can be open-ended (low displacement) or closed-end (displacement), allows inspection, can be filled with concrete. Drilled shafts (bored piles): large diameter (0.6 to 3.0 m), high axial and lateral capacity, can socket into rock, no vibration, but requires casing in caving ground and wet concrete placement. CFA (continuous flight auger): fast, low vibration, good in soft to medium ground, limited depth (typically < 25 m). Micropiles: small diameter (150 to 300 mm), grouted, for restricted access or underpinning, limited axial capacity per pile.

Estimate required pile length. Penetrate through compressible layers to bearing stratum. End-bearing: pile tip in rock or very dense soil. Friction: develop capacity along shaft in competent soil/rock. Typical target: factor of safety 2.0 to 2.5 on ultimate capacity for static analysis, 2.0 for pile load test-verified design.

Check site constraints. Vibration limits for adjacent structures (peak particle velocity < 50 mm/s for normal structures, < 12 mm/s for sensitive). Noise limits if residential area. Headroom restrictions (limited-access rigs, sectional casings). Spoil disposal for bored piles (volume = pi/4 * D^2 * L per pile). Contaminated ground: sealed system (CFA) or containment.

Preliminary cost comparison. Unit rate per linear meter installed, including mobilization, testing. Compare total foundation cost for each viable option. Consider schedule: driven piles are fast (10 to 20 per day for a typical crew); drilled shafts are slower (1 to 3 per day for large diameter).

steps.description: Calculate axial capacity of piles in compression and tension using appropriate methods for the selected pile type and ground.

inputs.name: selected-pile-type
inputs.desc: Pile type, dimensions, and installation method

inputs.name: ground-conditions
inputs.desc: Soil/rock parameters by depth: su, phi', Ko, SPT N, CPT qt

outputs.name: axial-capacity
outputs.desc: Ultimate shaft resistance, base resistance, and total capacity in compression and tension per pile

outputs.name: pile-length-required
outputs.desc: Required pile length to achieve target capacity with specified factor of safety

process: Calculate shaft resistance. In clay (undrained, alpha method): qs = alpha * su, where alpha = 0.55 for su/sigma_v' <= 1.0, reducing for higher su/sigma_v' ratios (API method). In sand (beta method): qs = beta * sigma_v', where beta = K * tan(delta), K depends on installation (1.0 for bored, 1.2 to 2.0 for driven displacement), delta = phi' minus 5 degrees. In rock: qs from rock socket methods (Horvath and Kenney: qs = 0.65 * sqrt(UCS) in MPa for normal roughness). Integrate shaft resistance over pile length: Qs = sum(qs_i * pi * D * dz_i).

Calculate base resistance. In clay: qb = Nc * su at tip (Nc = 9 for deep piles, D/B > 5). In sand: qb limited by CPT-based methods (Eslami-Fellenius: qb = average of qt in influence zone, typically 4D below to 8D above tip, with geometric averaging). For rock socket: qb = bearing capacity factor * UCS (typically 2.5 to 5.0 * UCS for intact rock, reduced for fractured). Qb = qb * Ab.

For CPT direct methods (preferred when CPT data available): use LCPC method or UniCone method. LCPC: shaft resistance from qt with empirical factors by soil type (clay, sand, gravel). Base resistance from average qt near tip with correction factor. These methods have the best calibration to pile load test databases.

Calculate tension capacity. Shaft resistance in tension is typically 75% of compression shaft resistance (reduced for clays due to changes in effective stress during pullout). No base resistance contribution. Check structural capacity of pile in tension (connections, splices).

Apply factors of safety. LRFD approach (AASHTO): phi factors depend on analysis method and site variability. Static analysis only: phi = 0.45 (shaft) and 0.40 (tip). With static load test: phi = 0.70 to 0.80. With dynamic testing (CAPWAP signal matching): phi = 0.65. ASD approach: FS = 2.0 with load test, 2.5 to 3.0 without.

steps.description: Analyze pile response to lateral loads using p-y curve or equivalent methods.

inputs.name: structural-loads
inputs.desc: Lateral loads and moments at pile head from structural analysis

inputs.name: ground-conditions
inputs.desc: Soil properties for lateral analysis (su, phi', subgrade modulus by depth)

outputs.name: lateral-response
outputs.desc: Pile head deflection, maximum bending moment and its depth, and shear force profile

outputs.name: structural-demand
outputs.desc: Required pile section for combined axial and lateral loading

process: Select analysis method. P-y curve method: nonlinear springs along pile length representing soil resistance. Standard p-y curves: soft clay (Matlock 1970), stiff clay (Reese et al. 1975), sand (Reese et al. 1974, API 2000). P-y curves define ultimate lateral resistance and load-deflection shape as function of depth, soil properties, and pile diameter.

Build p-y model. Discretize pile into segments (0.25 to 0.5 m spacing). Assign p-y curves based on soil type at each depth. Pile properties: EI (may be cracked section for concrete piles), length. Boundary conditions at head: free (moment = applied moment, shear = applied lateral load) or fixed (rotation = 0 for pile cap connection). Solve iteratively (nonlinear springs require iteration to converge).

Check results. Pile head deflection: typically limited to 6 to 25 mm depending on structure tolerance. Maximum bending moment: occurs at 3 to 8 pile diameters below ground surface in most soils. Compare to pile structural capacity (Mn for concrete, Mp for steel). Shear force profile: check maximum shear against structural capacity.

For pile groups: group reduction factors (p-multipliers) from Reese and Van Impe or Brown et al. Leading row: p-multiplier = 0.8 to 1.0. Second row: 0.4 to 0.7. Third and subsequent rows: 0.3 to 0.6. Depends on pile spacing (greater reduction at closer spacing, typically S/D < 5). Apply p-multipliers to p-y curves for each row and analyze the group.

Combined loading check. For reinforced concrete piles: construct M-N interaction diagram including pile self-weight. Check that (M, N) at every depth lies within the interaction surface. For steel piles: combined stress check per AISC (Pu/Pn + Mu/Mn <= 1.0 for small axial, bilinear interaction for larger). If pile section is insufficient, increase pile size or add piles to reduce per-pile demand.

steps.description: Plan and execute pile load tests to verify design capacity and integrity tests to confirm construction quality.

inputs.name: axial-capacity
inputs.desc: Predicted capacity to be verified by testing

inputs.name: selected-pile-type
inputs.desc: Pile type and expected construction quality indicators

outputs.name: load-test-results
outputs.desc: Measured load-settlement curve, ultimate capacity, and comparison to prediction

outputs.name: integrity-test-results
outputs.desc: Pile integrity confirmation: length, cross-section continuity, concrete quality

process: Plan static load test. Test pile loaded to 200% of design load (ASTM D1143 for compression, D3689 for tension). Reaction system: anchor piles (minimum 5 diameters clear from test pile), or kentledge (dead weight). Maintained load procedure: apply load in increments (25% of design load), hold each for 2 to 15 minutes, hold 200% for 12 to 24 hours. Quick maintained load: 5-minute holds (faster, less creep data). Instrumentation: dial gauges or LVDTs on reference beams, load cell or calibrated jack, tell-tales for tip settlement, strain gauges for load distribution.

Interpret static load test. Plot load-settlement curve. Determine ultimate capacity: Davisson offset method (line parallel to elastic compression, offset by 3.8 + D/120 mm from origin, intersection with load-settlement curve gives ultimate). Or 10% of pile diameter settlement criterion. Compare measured to predicted: if measured > predicted, design is verified and phi factor can be increased. If measured < predicted, investigate (may need longer piles or redesign).

Plan dynamic testing. High-strain dynamic testing (PDA, pile driving analyzer): measures force and velocity at pile head during driving or restrike. Signal matching analysis (CAPWAP) estimates shaft and base resistance distribution. Test during initial driving for driveability assessment and on restrike (minimum 24 hours for setup) for capacity verification. Test at least 2% of production piles (minimum 2 per site).

Plan Statnamic testing (alternative to static for large piles). Rapid load applied by combustion gases launching a reaction mass. Duration 100 to 200 ms. Measured force, displacement, acceleration. Unloading point method to derive static capacity from dynamic data. Accounts for rate effects and inertia. Suitable for drilled shafts where static load test reaction is impractical.

Plan integrity testing. Cross-hole sonic logging (CSL) for drilled shafts: PVC access tubes cast into pile, ultrasonic pulse between tubes measures concrete quality and continuity. Minimum 3 tubes for piles < 1.5 m diameter, 4 for larger. Test at 2 to 7 days after casting. Thermal integrity profiling (TIP): temperature measurement in access tubes during concrete hydration (defects cause temperature anomalies). Low-strain integrity testing (PIT/sonic echo): for all pile types, detects major defects (necks, cracks, base quality) from wave reflection. Test 100% of drilled shafts (CSL), 10 to 20% of driven piles (PIT).

description: Build and manage a construction schedule from WBS through CPM analysis, resource loading, earned value tracking, and field execution.

steps.description: Develop the work breakdown structure and define schedulable activities with durations and dependencies.

inputs.name: project-scope
inputs.desc: Contract scope, drawings, specifications, and quantity takeoff

inputs.name: construction-method
inputs.desc: Selected construction methods and equipment for major work items

outputs.name: activity-list
outputs.desc: Complete list of activities with ID, description, duration, and predecessors/successors

outputs.name: wbs-structure
outputs.desc: Hierarchical WBS with cost accounts linked to activities

process: Decompose scope into WBS. Level 1: project. Level 2: major areas or phases (site preparation, foundations, structure, MEP, finishes, commissioning). Level 3: disciplines or systems within each area. Level 4: work packages (smallest scope element assigned to a single responsible party). Level 5: activities (schedulable tasks within work packages). Ensure every scope item is captured (compare WBS to specification sections and drawing sheets).

Define activities. Each activity must have: clear start and completion criteria, a single responsible party, a measurable deliverable, and a duration estimable from production rates. Avoid activities longer than 20 working days (break into smaller pieces for control). Avoid activities shorter than 1 day (aggregate for manageability). Typical project: 500 to 5,000 activities depending on size and complexity.

Estimate durations. Production rate method: duration = quantity / (crew size * daily production rate * efficiency factor). Use historical data, RS Means, or subcontractor input for rates. Account for weather: rain days per month from historical records, cold weather productivity reduction (below -10 C: 50% for outdoor concrete, 75% for earthwork). Add mobilization and demobilization time.

Define logic relationships. Finish-to-Start (FS): most common, successor starts when predecessor finishes. Start-to-Start (SS): activities start together (parallel work, e.g., excavation and shoring). Finish-to-Finish (FF): activities finish together (e.g., MEP rough-in and inspection). Lags: positive lag for curing time (FS+7d for concrete cure before form strip). Avoid negative lags (leads); restructure logic instead.

Include constraints and milestones. Contractual milestones (substantial completion date, sectional completion). External constraints (material delivery dates, permit dates, utility shutdowns, road closures). Physical constraints (concrete pour sequence, crane reach limitations, tower crane climbing schedule). Weather windows (no earthwork in spring thaw, no roofing in winter).

steps.description: Perform critical path method analysis, identify the critical path, and optimize the schedule to meet the contract completion date.

inputs.name: activity-list
inputs.desc: Activities with durations and logic relationships

inputs.name: wbs-structure
inputs.desc: WBS for organizing and reporting

outputs.name: baseline-schedule
outputs.desc: CPM schedule with early/late dates, total float, and identified critical path

outputs.name: schedule-optimization
outputs.desc: Compression options (crashing, fast-tracking) with cost and risk implications

process: Forward pass. Start from project start date. For each activity: Early Start (ES) = maximum Early Finish of all predecessors (plus lag). Early Finish (EF) = ES + duration. Work through network from start to finish. The Early Finish of the last activity is the calculated project completion date.

Backward pass. Start from project completion date (or contract date if it is the target). For each activity: Late Finish (LF) = minimum Late Start of all successors (minus lag). Late Start (LS) = LF - duration. Work backward from finish to start.

Calculate float. Total Float (TF) = LS - ES = LF - EF. Activities with TF = 0 are on the critical path. Free Float = minimum (ES of successors) - EF. Near-critical paths (TF < 10 days) need attention as they can become critical with minor delays.

Optimize if calculated completion exceeds target. Crashing: add resources to critical path activities to shorten duration. Cost-slope analysis: crash cost minus normal cost divided by normal duration minus crash duration. Crash activities with lowest cost slope first. Fast-tracking: overlap sequential activities (change FS to SS with lag). Increases risk of rework. Evaluate each option for cost, risk, and practical feasibility.

Validate schedule quality. Check metrics: no open ends (every activity has predecessor and successor except start/finish milestones), no negative float, reasonable float distribution, critical path is logical, no excessive use of constraints (which mask logic issues), no dangling logic. Schedule density: 2 to 4 relationships per activity is typical. Resource-load and check for over-allocation.

steps.description: Assign resources (labor, equipment, materials) to activities and level resource demands to feasible rates.

inputs.name: baseline-schedule
inputs.desc: CPM schedule with dates and float

inputs.name: project-scope
inputs.desc: Quantity takeoff and crew compositions for each work type

outputs.name: resource-loaded-schedule
outputs.desc: Schedule with labor, equipment, and material curves showing peak demands

outputs.name: resource-plan
outputs.desc: Crew mobilization plan, equipment procurement schedule, and material delivery schedule

process: Assign labor resources. Define crew compositions for each activity type (e.g., concrete pour: 1 foreman, 6 laborers, 2 finishers, 1 pump operator). Calculate daily labor demand from overlapping activities. Plot total labor histogram. Identify peaks that exceed available or practical workforce.

Level resources. Shift non-critical activities within their float to reduce peak demand. Priority: delay activities with most float first (preserve near-critical paths). If leveling within float is insufficient, accept the peak (with overtime/additional crews) or extend the schedule (if float is available on overall project). Target smooth S-curve for cumulative labor: rapid ramp-up is expensive (mobilization, training), so aim for gradual buildup.

Plan equipment. Long-lead equipment: tower cranes (procurement 12 to 16 weeks), specialized formwork systems, TBMs. Schedule crane availability to match structural erection. Plan crane locations, reach, and capacity for lifting requirements. Earthmoving fleet: match fleet size to daily production rate needed for schedule.

Plan material deliveries. Long-lead materials: structural steel (fabrication 8 to 16 weeks after approval), precast concrete (8 to 12 weeks), custom mechanical equipment. Just-in-time delivery for high-volume materials (concrete, rebar, drywall) to minimize site storage. Procurement schedule: back-calculate from need date minus fabrication time minus approval time minus shop drawing preparation.

Generate cash flow projection. Distribute cost to activities (cost-loaded schedule). Plot cumulative cost curve (S-curve). Monthly billing projection from work completed. Early cash flow for mobilization, late peak for MEP and finishes. Use this for project financing (draw schedule against construction loan).

steps.description: Track schedule performance during construction using earned value management and manage field execution with look-ahead schedules.

inputs.name: resource-loaded-schedule
inputs.desc: Baseline schedule with cost and resource loading

inputs.name: resource-plan
inputs.desc: Planned labor, equipment, and material procurement

outputs.name: performance-metrics
outputs.desc: SPI, CPI, and EAC at each reporting period with trend analysis

outputs.name: recovery-actions
outputs.desc: Schedule recovery plan if behind, with specific actions, revised dates, and resource adjustments

process: Update schedule at regular intervals (weekly for active construction, bi-weekly for early stages). Record: actual start and finish dates, remaining duration for in-progress activities, percent complete based on quantity installed (not time elapsed). Recalculate CPM with actuals to get projected completion date.

Calculate earned value metrics. BCWS (Planned Value, PV): budgeted cost of work scheduled to date. BCWP (Earned Value, EV): budgeted cost of work actually performed to date. ACWP (Actual Cost, AC): actual cost incurred to date. SPI = EV/PV (< 1.0 means behind schedule). CPI = EV/AC (< 1.0 means over budget). EAC (Estimate at Completion) = BAC/CPI for systemic overruns, or AC + ETC for re-estimated remaining work.

Three-week look-ahead schedule. Extract activities planned to start or be in progress during the next three weeks. Break into daily or shift-level tasks. Assign specific crews and equipment. Identify constraints: preceding work completion, material availability, inspection holds, weather. Resolve constraints before the work week starts. This is the foreman's working schedule.

Monitor critical path. If critical path activities fall behind, the project completion date slips. Recovery options: increase crews on critical activities, work overtime (productivity drops 10% for 50-hour week, 20% for 60-hour), re-sequence to create parallel work, change construction method. Document delays: contemporaneous recording of delay events, categorize as excusable (weather, owner changes) or non-excusable (contractor performance).

Prepare monthly schedule narrative. Compare progress to baseline. Explain variances: causes of delay or acceleration. Show status of critical and near-critical paths. Present 3-month rolling forecast. If behind, present recovery plan with specific actions and revised completion date. This narrative supports progress payment applications and delay claims.

description: Conduct an environmental impact assessment from scoping through baseline surveys, impact evaluation, mitigation design, and EIS documentation.

steps.description: Define the scope of the environmental assessment and conduct baseline environmental surveys.

inputs.name: project-description
inputs.desc: Proposed project: location, footprint, construction methods, operational characteristics

inputs.name: regulatory-framework
inputs.desc: Applicable environmental regulations (NEPA, state CEQA, EU EIA Directive, etc.)

outputs.name: scoping-report

process: Screen the project. Determine if EIA is required (thresholds vary by jurisdiction: NEPA for federal action, state CEQA/SEPA for state involvement, EU EIA Directive Annex I mandatory / Annex II screening). Determine level of assessment: Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) for significant impacts, Environmental Assessment (EA) for uncertain significance, Categorical Exclusion if clearly no impact.

Conduct scoping. Identify all environmental topics potentially affected: air quality, noise and vibration, water resources (surface and ground), ecology (habitats, species), landscape and visual, cultural heritage, traffic and transport, socioeconomic, human health, climate (greenhouse gas emissions), cumulative effects. Scoping consultation with regulatory agencies and public to identify key concerns. Define study area for each topic (noise: typically 500 m from works, ecology: wider for mobile species).

Conduct baseline surveys. Ecology: Phase 1 habitat survey (extended to UK NVC or equivalent classification), protected species surveys (bat, bird, reptile, amphibian, botanical) timed to survey seasons. Air quality: diffusion tube monitoring for NO2 (minimum 3 months, ideally 12), PM10/PM2.5 monitoring if near sensitive receptors. Noise: attended and unattended noise monitoring at representative receptor locations (minimum 1 week continuous, capturing weekday and weekend). Water: river flow and quality monitoring, groundwater level monitoring. Traffic: classified traffic counts on affected roads.

Document baseline. For each topic, describe existing conditions quantitatively where possible. Identify sensitive receptors (residential properties, schools, hospitals, protected habitats, listed buildings, watercourses). Map receptor locations and distances from the project. Identify any existing environmental issues (exceedances of air quality standards, degraded habitats, contaminated land).

Define assessment methodology for each topic. Significance = f(magnitude of impact, sensitivity of receptor). Use standardized matrices (e.g., IEMA guidelines, DMRB for transport). Define magnitude categories (negligible, minor, moderate, major) with quantitative thresholds where possible (e.g., noise: < 1 dB negligible, 1-3 dB minor, 3-5 dB moderate, > 5 dB major change). Define sensitivity categories for receptors.

steps.description: Assess the magnitude of environmental impacts using appropriate models and methods for each topic.

inputs.name: scoping-report
inputs.desc: Topics to assess with methodologies

inputs.name: baseline-conditions
inputs.desc: Existing environmental conditions

outputs.name: impact-assessment
outputs.desc: Predicted impacts by topic with significance ratings before and after mitigation

outputs.name: cumulative-effects
outputs.desc: Assessment of combined effects with other planned or existing projects

process: Noise assessment. Construction: predict noise levels at receptors from equipment sound power levels and distance attenuation (BS 5228 or FHWA RCNM). Calculate daily LAeq at each receptor. Compare to baseline and to threshold criteria (e.g., 75 dB LAeq at facade for significant effect during daytime construction). Operational: road traffic noise from traffic flow (CRTN, TNM, or FHWA model), rail noise from pass-by events (CRN), industrial noise from fixed plant (ISO 9613-2 propagation with meteorological correction).

Air quality assessment. Construction dust: qualitative risk assessment (IAQM guidance: site size, distance to receptors, dust-generating activities). Operational: atmospheric dispersion modeling (AERMOD for point and area sources, ADMS-Roads for road traffic). Input: emission rates from traffic data and emission factors (EFT, EMFAC), meteorological data (minimum 5 years hourly), terrain, buildings. Output: predicted concentrations of NO2, PM10, PM2.5 at receptors. Compare to air quality standards (NAAQS, EU limit values).

Ecology assessment. Habitat loss: calculate area of each habitat type lost, compare to local/regional extent. Assign value to habitats (international, national, county, local, negligible). For protected species: assess disturbance, displacement, mortality, barrier effects. Population-level impact assessment where possible (e.g., collision risk modeling for birds at wind farms). For aquatic ecology: water quality impact on fish and invertebrates.

Water resources assessment. Surface water: pollutant runoff modeling (simple event mean concentration or SWMM for complex), flood risk assessment (hydraulic modeling if development in floodplain), geomorphological impact on channel. Groundwater: dewatering impact assessment (drawdown prediction from pumping test data), contamination risk from construction activities, impact on groundwater-dependent ecosystems.

Cumulative effects. Identify other projects within the zone of influence (planning registers, infrastructure plans). Assess combined effects on each receptor: total noise from this project plus others, total traffic increase, combined habitat loss. In-combination effects for European designated sites (Habitats Regulations Assessment). Climate change: total GHG emissions in construction and operation (tonnes CO2e per year, compared to national/sectoral budgets).

steps.description: Design mitigation measures to reduce significant impacts and a monitoring program to verify effectiveness.

inputs.name: impact-assessment
inputs.desc: Predicted impacts with significance ratings

inputs.name: baseline-conditions
inputs.desc: Baseline for monitoring comparison

outputs.name: mitigation-measures
outputs.desc: Specific mitigation for each significant impact, following the hierarchy: avoid, minimize, restore, offset

outputs.name: monitoring-program
outputs.desc: Monitoring parameters, locations, frequency, trigger levels, and contingency actions

process: Apply mitigation hierarchy. Avoid: modify project design to eliminate the impact (realign route to avoid habitat, relocate noisy operations away from receptors). Minimize: reduce the magnitude (noise barriers, dust suppression, silt fences, working hours restrictions). Restore: return affected area to pre-project condition (habitat reinstatement, landscaping). Offset: compensate for residual impacts elsewhere (biodiversity offsetting, carbon credits). Avoid is always preferred; offset is last resort.

Noise mitigation. Construction: best practical means (BPM): low-noise equipment, acoustic enclosures, barriers, restricted working hours (typically 07:00-19:00 weekdays, 07:00-13:00 Saturday, no Sunday/holiday), section 61 consent (UK) or noise variance (US). Operational: noise barriers (insertion loss from Maekawa formula: IL = 10*log(3+20*N) dB, where N is Fresnel number), low-noise road surface (3 to 5 dB reduction), building insulation for residual exceedances.

Ecology mitigation. Timing restrictions (avoid bird nesting season March-August, bat hibernation November-March for northern hemisphere). Translocation of protected species (great crested newts, reptiles) to receptor sites prepared in advance. Habitat creation: like-for-like or better replacement at specified ratio (2:1 or 3:1 for high-value habitat). Wildlife crossings: underpasses, overpasses, ledges in culverts for otters. Long-term management plan for created habitats (minimum 30 years).

Water mitigation. Construction: settlement ponds for site runoff, spill containment for fuel and chemical storage, wheel wash to prevent mud on roads. Operational: sustainable drainage systems (SuDS): swales, detention basins, permeable paving, constructed wetlands. Design to treat and attenuate runoff to greenfield rates for all events up to 1-in-100-year plus climate change allowance.

Design monitoring program. Pre-construction: confirm baseline and establish reference conditions. During construction: noise monitoring at nearest receptors (continuous where predicted to exceed thresholds), dust monitoring (PM10 or visual), water quality at discharge points, ecological watching brief during site clearance. Post-construction: habitat establishment monitoring (annual for 5 years minimum), noise compliance monitoring, water quality. Define trigger levels and contingency actions: if trigger exceeded, implement additional mitigation within defined response time.

steps.description: Compile the Environmental Impact Statement, manage public and agency review, and prepare responses to comments.

inputs.name: impact-assessment
inputs.desc: Completed impact assessments for all topics

inputs.name: mitigation-measures
inputs.desc: Designed mitigation and monitoring program

outputs.name: environmental-impact-statement
outputs.desc: Complete EIS document with non-technical summary, ready for submission

outputs.name: comment-responses
outputs.desc: Responses to public and agency comments with any assessment revisions

process: Structure the EIS. Non-Technical Summary (NTS): plain language, illustrated, standalone document that the public can understand. Main document chapters: Introduction (project need, alternatives considered), Project Description, Assessment Methodology, Baseline Conditions, Assessment of Effects (one chapter per topic), Mitigation and Monitoring, Cumulative Effects, Summary of Residual Effects. Technical appendices: survey reports, modeling data, consultation records.

Write clearly. Each topic chapter: describe baseline, describe impact pathways, state predicted impact magnitude, state receptor sensitivity, derive significance. Use consistent terminology (the significance matrix). Present results in summary tables (receptor, impact, magnitude, sensitivity, significance before mitigation, mitigation measure, residual significance). Be honest about uncertainty: state confidence level in predictions, identify assumptions.

Alternatives analysis. NEPA requires analysis of alternatives including no-action. Present alternatives genuinely considered: route alternatives, technology alternatives, timing alternatives. Explain why each was selected or rejected based on environmental, technical, and economic factors. The preferred alternative should emerge from the comparison, not be predetermined.

Submit for review. Public notice of availability (Federal Register for NEPA, local newspapers). Review period: minimum 45 days for EIS (NEPA), 30 days for EA. Public hearing if required or requested. Agency review: cooperating agencies (USFWS for endangered species, USACE for wetlands, SHPO for cultural resources).

Respond to comments. Categorize comments by topic. Prepare substantive responses to each unique comment. If comments identify new information or errors: revise the assessment, prepare supplemental EIS if changes are significant. Compile responses into a final EIS or Record of Decision (ROD). The ROD states the decision, identifies the selected alternative, and commits to the mitigation measures.
